dek_candidates: A Mumbai infrastructure contractor that builds railway works, bridges and roads, and runs a ready-mix concrete plant in Thane district. Here is what its draft red herring prospectus discloses about the offer, five years of accounts, and the risks it names itself.
Two segments, one dominant customer, and a working-capital raise. A page-by-page read of A B Infrabuild Limited's draft prospectus.

beats.beat: Start with the plain version: this is a contractor that bids for government civil-works tenders, executes them, and bills the government. The second engine is a concrete plant that supplies ready-mix concrete, the pre-mixed material poured into formwork on construction sites.

The infrastructure work is described in three named service lines: railways (designing and building platforms, station buildings, gauge conversion and laying tracks), bridges (beam, cantilever, arch, suspension, cable-stayed and truss bridges), and roadways (bituminous and concrete roads connecting highways and district roads).

The concrete business is a single facility: a ready mix concrete plant at Kashimira, in Thane district, Maharashtra, which the filing describes as its state-of-the-art equipment and quality-control site. That plant is the company's only disclosed physical operating footprint in the excerpts.

Contracts are won by tender, and the filing sets out the six-step sequence: a client floats the tender; a pre-bid meeting resolves queries; the contractor bids; the job is awarded to the lowest quote and a letter of acceptance goes to the lowest bidder; the contractor deposits a performance guarantee; drawings are issued and the site is handed over. There is no negotiation on price in this model — the lowest number wins.

The client list is almost entirely public bodies: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Western Railway, Central Railway, Mumbai Railway Vikas Corporation Ltd, Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority and the Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India Ltd, plus private names including Sky Way Infrastructure, Dev Engineers, GCC Hotel and Krypton Corp.
Western Railway is not a customer among many. The filing says it has been a client since 2006 and has been a major contributor to revenue.
The concentration shows up twice in the filing. Western Railway accounts for 52% of the orders on hand, and revenue from key customers for the year ended March 31, 2018 was 57% of total revenue.
Geographically the company says it is a major player in Mumbai and is consolidating its position in Maharashtra. It does not describe operations outside the state.

One technical detail the company puts forward as a strength: it uses box pushing, a technique for driving a concrete box under an existing railway line or road without cutting through the traffic above it. It matters because it is the kind of capability that suits railway work in a dense city.

business.heading: What the company does
business.purpose: Explain the two revenue engines, how work is actually won, who the customers are, and how concentrated the book is.

beats.beat: The filing presents five years of restated financials, from FY2014 to FY2018, in ₹ lakhs. Read in ₹ crore, two patterns stand out: revenue is shrinking, and profit is not shrinking with it — it is moving around for reasons the top line does not explain.

Revenue from operations, in ₹ crore, runs ₹86.61 (FY2014), ₹90.21 (FY2015), ₹74.53 (FY2016), ₹73.44 (FY2017) and ₹60.53 (FY2018). That is a fall of roughly a third from the FY2015 peak to FY2018. In lakhs, the filing's own words: ₹9,021.12 lakhs in FY2015 down to ₹6,053.05 lakhs in FY2018.

Profit before interest, depreciation and tax — the filing's EBITDA line — in ₹ crore: ₹7.84 (FY2014), ₹9.46 (FY2015), ₹7.83 (FY2016), ₹6.76 (FY2017) and ₹9.29 (FY2018). Note the shape: EBITDA in FY2018 is the second-highest of the five years while revenue is the lowest, so margin, not volume, carried the year.

Profit after tax, in ₹ crore: ₹0.96 (FY2014), ₹0.78 (FY2015), ₹0.33 (FY2016), ₹0.16 (FY2017) and ₹3.15 (FY2018). The FY2018 figure is a jump from ₹15.86 lakhs to ₹314.66 lakhs — nearly twenty times the prior year — and that single swing is the most important number in the financial section for a reader to interrogate.
Total assets, in ₹ crore: ₹70.62 (FY2014), ₹72.67 (FY2015), ₹62.95 (FY2016), ₹75.37 (FY2017) and ₹82.32 (FY2018). The asset base grew in each of the last two years even as revenue fell.

The debt picture has two halves pointing in opposite directions. Long-term borrowings fell from ₹5.87 crore in FY2014 to ₹1.33 crore in FY2018. Short-term borrowings rose from ₹30.82 crore in FY2014 to ₹35.37 crore in FY2018. The filing's own note records short-term borrowings rising from ₹3,082.27 lakhs in FY2014 to ₹3,537.35 lakhs in FY2018.
Put on one line, long plus short-term borrowings were about ₹36.70 crore at FY2018 — against ₹82.32 crore of total assets. The borrowing has been shifted to the short end rather than retired.

On cash, the filing says the company had negative cash flow in recent financial years and warns that sustained negative cash flow could hurt the business and results of operations. It also flags that failure to recover money from sundry debtors and trade receivables in time could affect its financial condition.

One thing to be explicit about: the excerpts do not carry the year-by-year cash flow statement, so operating, investing and financing cash figures cannot be reported here. The filing's own statement that cash flow was negative is what is available.

financials.heading: Five years of accounts, restated
financials.purpose: Take the reader through the revenue, profit, EBITDA, asset and debt lines period by period — the section the filing most rewards careful reading on.

beats.beat: Control is concentrated in one person. Amit Bholanath Mishra is the promoter and holds 74,95,476 equity shares, or 90.949% of the pre-issue paid-up capital.
The other directors hold almost nothing: Bharat kumar Parmar 300 shares, Shree Prakash Singh 300 shares and Mukesh Pandey 300 shares, as whole-time directors.
One further holder is named: Mr. Hatim Sakerwala holds 9% of the equity shares as on the date of the draft, listed under key management personnel shareholding.

The named key management is young and thin. The chief financial officer, Ms. Anchal Pachori, is 28 and a chartered accountant. The company secretary and compliance officer, Mr. Mohit Soni, is 26 and an associate member of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India.

Related-party dealings are recurring and disclosed in number: ₹68.4 lakhs of loans taken from key management personnel or the board in FY2018, ₹57.7 lakhs of director remuneration in FY2018, and ₹324.3 lakhs of outstanding payables to related parties as on 31 March 2018. The filing separately warns that it has entered into related party transactions in the past and may continue to do so.

On clean-record statements, the filing says none of the directors are on the RBI list of willful defaulters, that no criminal cases or investigations are pending against any director, and that the promoter has confirmed he has not been declared a willful defaulter. Against that, the filing states that the company, its promoter and directors are currently involved in litigation pending at various stages.

Two promoter-linked companies were struck off by the Registrar of Companies for non-operation of business: Al-Noor Chickens Private Limited on March 12, 2016 and A B Magma Automobiles Private Limited on March 11, 2016.

Add the governance items already noted in the offer section, because they belong here too: shares issued in the last 12 months at a price that may be below the issue price, no independent appraisal of the project, and no monitoring agency for the use of proceeds.

beats.beat: The sector is Indian infrastructure and construction, which the filing defines broadly to include power, bridges, dams, roads and urban infrastructure development.

The structure of the market is the important part for a small contractor. The filing calls it highly fragmented and working capital intensive, contributing roughly 8% of India's GDP at constant prices. Fragmented means many bidders chasing the same tenders, which is why price is competed down.

The demand case rests on government spending programmes: 100 Smart Cities, AMRUT, Make in India and Power for All, plus eased foreign direct investment norms across 15 sectors including real estate and construction development.

The size numbers the filing cites: India needs ₹50 trillion, or about US$777.73 billion, of infrastructure investment by 2022 to sustain development; the logistics sector is projected to grow at a 10.5% CAGR from US$160 billion in 2017 to US$215 billion by 2020; and construction development drew US$24.67 billion of FDI between April 2000 and December 2017.

The macro backdrop the filing offers: cumulative growth in the index of eight core industries was 4.2% in 2017-18, India's GDP growth was expected to stay above 7% in 2017, the working-age population is expected to reach 64% by 2021, and infrastructure spending was 9.0% of GDP in the 12th Five-Year Plan.

On competition, the filing says only that the industry is competitive with players in both the organised and unorganised sectors. It names no competitor. That is a real limit on what a reader can conclude about relative position.

The headwinds the company lists against itself are worth repeating in its own framing: slow pace of government projects, working capital crunch that may affect profitability, and changes in government policies.

Regulation is a live operating constraint rather than background: the Companies Act 2013, GST on supply of goods and services, the Factories Act 1948 for labour in factories, and environmental statutes including the Water and Air pollution Acts and the Environment Protection Act 1986.

industry.heading: The market it operates in

beats.beat: A B Infrabuild is a Mumbai-area infrastructure contractor. It builds railway works, bridges and roads for government clients, and it also runs a ready-mix concrete plant. Those are the two things it does; everything else in the filing is detail on top of them.
The filing describes the business as exactly two segments: creation of infrastructure, and operating a ready mix concrete plant.
The offer is 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 face value each, at an issue price the filing leaves blank as ₹[•]. So the number of shares is fixed; the amount raised is not yet public.

For scale: the company earned ₹60.53 crore of revenue in FY2018 (₹6,053.05 lakhs) and made ₹3.15 crore of profit, so this is a small company by the standards of the main board, and the filing has to be read at that scale.

intro.purpose: Orient a reader who has never heard of the company: what it builds, what it is selling, and why the size of the raise matters relative to its own balance sheet.

beats.beat: A public issue can be a fresh issue, where the company creates new shares and keeps the money, or an offer for sale, where existing owners sell their shares and the company gets nothing. The excerpts supplied for this report do not state which this is, or in what proportion, so the report must say that plainly rather than assume the usual mix.
What is disclosed: 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 face value each, at an issue price left as ₹[•].

There are two objects of the issue. The first is specific: ₹1,130 lakhs, or ₹11.30 crore, to meet working capital requirements. The second is general corporate purposes, with the amount left as a blank in the filing.

Why working capital is the named object: this is a business that pays for labour, materials and performance guarantees before the client pays it. The filing separately discloses ₹405.02 lakhs of unsecured loans outstanding as on March 31, 2018 that are repayable on demand.
The issue is managed by Mark Corporate Advisors Private Limited as lead manager, with Bigshare Services Private Limited as registrar.

Two accountability disclosures sit alongside the objects: no independent agency has been appointed to appraise the proposed project, and no monitoring agency has been appointed, leaving deployment of funds to management and the board with oversight by the audit committee.
The filing also notes that the company issued equity shares in the last 12 months at a price which may be lower than the issue price. It does not state the earlier price.

offer.heading: The offer and where the money goes
offer.purpose: Set out the mechanics of the issue, the two objects of the raise, and the accountability gaps the filing itself flags.

beats.beat: One customer. The filing states that the majority of revenues will depend on Indian Railways, its largest customer, contributing 57% of revenue in Fiscal 2018, and that losing it would cause a significant dip in revenues. The order book points the same way: Western Railway alone is 52% of orders on hand. A reader should treat this single relationship as the swing factor in the entire business.

The revenue model depends on winning bids, and the process awards to the lowest quote. The filing warns that revenues largely depend on acceptance of bids submitted to the government and government departments, that performance could suffer if bids are not awarded or are negotiated down, and that attempts to secure government and PSU projects may not always succeed.

Cash flow and a demand loan. The filing discloses negative cash flow in recent financial years and warns that sustained negative cash flow could hurt the business. It also discloses ₹405.02 lakhs of unsecured loans outstanding as on March 31, 2018 that are repayable on demand, and says a call on them could affect cash flow and financial condition. Slow recovery from trade receivables is flagged separately.

Geography. Revenue is concentrated in Mumbai, and the filing warns that adverse developments affecting operations in that region could hurt revenue and results. In a tender-driven business, a slowdown in one city's public works pipeline is not a diversifiable problem.

Cost overruns and order-book illusion. The filing warns that the company may see reduced profits or losses, or cancellations and deferrals, if contract costs rise above estimates, and states that contracts in the order book may be adjusted, cancelled or suspended by clients — so the order book is not necessarily indicative of future revenues or earnings.

risks.heading: The five risks that matter most
risks.purpose: Five company-specific risks, each explained, not a reprint of the risk factors chapter.

beats.beat: The usual way an IPO price is defended is by comparison. The company computes its own earnings per share, net asset value and return on net worth, puts them in a table beside the same figures for a set of listed peer companies, and argues that its price sits sensibly against theirs.

The filing follows this form. Its Basis for Issue Price section states that the issue price of ₹[•] is determined by the company in consultation with the lead manager and is justified based on the accounting ratios above, and that the issue price is [•] times the face value of ₹10 per share. Both blanks are left blank in the filing.

The section headed Comparison of Accounting Ratios with Peer Group Companies carries numeric values — including 3.82, 12.39, 28.14 and 44.71 across the extracted figures. The excerpts do not attach those values to named companies or label which column is which ratio.

The same limitation applies to the per-year ratios on the preceding page, which appear as pairs and trios by year — 1.31 and 1.31 for FY2015-16, 0.63 and 0.63 for FY2016-17, 12.59 and 3.82 for FY2017-18, and 4.14, 1.97 and 28.14 across the three years in a second block. Without the column headings, these cannot be assigned to EPS, NAV or RoNW with confidence, and the report should say so rather than guess.

So an implied price range cannot be built from this filing as excerpted. The mechanic would be straightforward — take the peer earnings multiple, apply it to this company's earnings per share, and you get an indicative value per share — but two inputs are missing: the peer companies are not named in the excerpts, and the issue price is redacted as ₹[•] in the filing itself. Stating the method and stating the missing inputs is the honest version of this section; filling the blanks would not be.

valuation-and-peers.purpose: Explain how an IPO price gets justified by comparison with peers, then show exactly how much of that comparison the excerpted filing actually supports.
